name: ArchGate
oneLiner: Architecture gate for .NET: {{term:roslyn}} analyzers that fail the build when code breaks the declared architecture — counted from the PR diff.
summary: Seven {{term:roslyn}} analyzers on `netstandard2.0` enforce part of the architectural constitution: the shared kernel boundary, persistence portability, controller/DbContext layering, orphan entities, inheritance instead of an interface, vendor SDK types leaking outside the adapter, a missing `AddServiceDefaults`. The gate counts **only the lines changed in a pull request** — without that, every new rule lights up thousands of warnings in existing code and the team switches the tool off in the first week; the problem is documented and reproduced on a two-commit repro. {{term:provenance|Provenance}} is read from real git — `git diff -U0` plus `git blame` plus commit trailers — never from code style, and it serves only to raise the severity threshold; it appears in the PR comment neither as a badge nor as a score. The whole thing ships as two `dotnet` tools — `ArchGate.Cli` and `ArchGate.CiComment`, the only two projects with `PackAsTool` — plus a third package, `ArchGate.Analyzers`, which is not a tool: it is a Roslyn analyzer package with `IncludeBuildOutput=false` whose DLL goes to `analyzers/dotnet/cs`. On top of that, a container image and a composite action.
tests: 150 [Fact] attributes across 21 files (`grep -rho '[Fact]' tests --include='*.cs' | wc -l`; zero `[Theory]`, zero `[InlineData]`); the ROADMAP says 146/146 and is two commits stale — the last change to `ROADMAP-archgate.md` is `716c32a`, and `git rev-list --count 716c32a..HEAD` gives 2 (one working commit and one merge). The tests were not run in this pass — no SDK in the environment.
ci: `archgate-pr-check.yml` runs the gate on the repository's own PRs; `release.yml` on a `v*` tag declares five jobs — `build`, `publish-nuget`, `publish-container`, `release-notes`, `moving-tag` — including verification of the packed analyzer in a temporary consumer project (a step inside `build`). No tag exists, so the release has never run for real.

components.name: ArchGate.Engine (Scanner)
components.description: Harness: parses every `.cs` file into a single compilation, runs the rule registry, maps diagnostics onto a violation record and works out the gate verdict. A neutral wrapper — run any set of analyzers over a directory and get deterministic JSON.

components.name: Provenance z historii gita
components.description: Line-by-line attribution from `git blame` and commit trailers, classified as Human/Ai/Mixed/Unknown. It tells an empty diff apart from a git failure, so the gate degrades to absolute mode instead of quietly letting things through.

components.name: Model konfiguracji konwencji
components.description: One configuration, two channels: the analyzer reads `.globalconfig`, the CLI reads `archgate.json` and flattens it onto the same keys — because an analyzer cannot open files under `EnforceExtendedAnalyzerRules`.

components.name: ArchGate.Rules (7 analysers)
components.description: The analyzers themselves are a general package for any C# repository, but the individual rules encode principles P1–P15 from the constitution — outside it, some of them have to be reconfigured.

components.name: ArchGate.CiComment
components.description: Renders the result to Markdown, works out the difference against the previous scan and updates **one** sticky PR comment, found by a hidden marker. Provenance deliberately never gets in there.

components.name: Composite GitHub Action
components.description: Deliberately composite rather than container-based — container actions only run on Linux runners. It checks that a base commit is present before turning on diff mode.

overlaps.reason: It does not invent its own rule language — it enforces principles P1–P15 from that repository and quotes them in the category of every diagnostic. The loop is closed.
The {{term:provenance}} signal is designed explicitly as a repudiation of that one: the specification cites per-session averaging as the mistake that must not be repeated.
The evidence discipline was carried over from there: the {{term:mutation|mutation run}} and the principle that a test suite which has never failed has not been tested.

product: The buyer is named outright: an engineering lead or a platform team in a .NET organisation that can see the debt from AI-written code growing and has nothing to measure it with. Open-core model, with an empty `enterprise/` directory waiting for team features. The problem sits in front of all of that, though: **the sales channel is blocked by the name**. Until that changes, this is a credibility artefact — a finished, documented, mutation-tested engine — and nothing more.
highlights: The repository knocked down its own marketing claim: the competitive document confirms a published namesake in the same package registry, corrects the numbers from two other people's reviews and **lists every place that went out of date as a result**. That is a rarer skill than writing an analyzer.

The release pipeline verifies the packed analyzer in a temporary consumer project and fails if the package does not emit a specific diagnostic. That catches the classic failure 'the DLL landed in the wrong folder, the package installs cleanly and does nothing'.

The analyzers deliberately sit on Roslyn 4.8.0 rather than 4.11.0, because an analyzer built against the newer one emits an error at the consumer. Established by consuming the packed `.nupkg`, not by reading the documentation.
Ten mutation variants of the rules, with tests that the real rule catches a case and the mutant lets it through — evidence that the tests respond to the mechanism and not to their own fixtures.
gaps: **Zero published artefacts.** There is no tag of any kind, so the three packages, the image and the action do not exist, and every install command in the README returns a 404. The README admits it, which is honest and does not change the fact.
Nine of the fifteen principles are not implemented, and four never will be — the tool covers 6/15 of the contract it appeals to.

The engine sees a single compilation parsed straight from files, with no MSBuildWorkspace and no package references — that makes some of the rules purely syntactic, which limits their accuracy and will require a rewrite once the constraint is lifted.
The repository is private, even though all of its distribution value depends on being public.
next: Decide on the new name and carry it through in **one pass**: repository name, three package identifiers, all the diagnostic identifiers, namespaces, `action.yml`, Dockerfile, documentation. The identifiers become an API contract the moment the first consumer types them into `.editorconfig` — after that point, changing them is breaking.
Fix the copyright line in LICENSE; it carries someone else's name, copied from another repository.
Cut the first tag under the new name and check whether the five release jobs actually pass — today they are unverified assumptions about secrets and package visibility.
Open the repository. A private CI gate has no way to win its first user.
Turn the gate on for the PRs of a consumer repository and fix the open entries — that is the only test that counts for the buyer.
risks: **A name collision with a published, maintained product in the same NuGet registry.** Publishing under the current name would read as a clone or a typosquat — and that is the one thing blocking the whole distribution path.
LICENSE assigns the rights to someone else's name, out of step with the rest of the configuration. In an MIT repository that is a legal defect, not a typo.
Many of the rules are matches on folder name and call shape, with no bound symbol — a risk of false positives, which the vision itself names as the known failure mode of this category of tool.
headline: Name taken by a working product in the same registry — the rename blocks all distribution
